title: The Clockmaker’s Apprentice
text:
The workshop stood at the end of a narrow lane, its window crowded with clocks that no longer agreed about the time. Inside, old Yusuf sat bent over his bench, a lens fixed in one eye, coaxing life back into mechanisms that most people would have thrown away. He had been mending clocks for more than fifty years, and he claimed he could tell what was wrong with one simply by listening to its tick.

Bilal came to him at fifteen, restless and impatient, sent by an uncle who hoped a trade would steady him. For the first month Yusuf gave him nothing to repair. He was told to clean parts, sort screws by size and sweep the floor. When Bilal complained that he was learning nothing, the old man handed him a stopped pocket watch and said, “Tell me why it has stopped. Do not touch it until you know.”

Bilal studied the watch for three days. He learned to look before acting, to notice a hair-thin bend in a spring or a speck of dust lodged between two teeth of a wheel. When at last he found the fault and set the watch ticking, Yusuf merely nodded, but Bilal understood that he had passed a test more important than any repair.

Years later, when customers brought their broken clocks to Bilal’s own shop, they often remarked on his calm. He never hurried and never guessed. He would listen, examine and only then pick up his tools. Asked where he had learned such patience, he would point to a small, battered pocket watch that still kept perfect time on the shelf above his bench.

title: Morning in the Old Bazaar
text:
The bazaar wakes before the sun. In the grey half-light, shutters rattle upward one after another, and shopkeepers sprinkle water on the dusty ground in front of their stalls to settle it for the day. A boy balances a tray of steaming glasses of tea on one palm as he threads his way between handcarts, calling out to regular customers by name. From somewhere deeper in the lanes comes the rhythmic clang of a coppersmith’s hammer.

By the time the first light touches the rooftops, the narrow street has become a river of colour. Bolts of cloth in saffron, crimson and emerald hang from the awnings of the drapers’ shops; pyramids of oranges and pomegranates glow on the fruit sellers’ carts; the spice merchants’ open sacks of turmeric, chilli and cumin fill the air with a scent so sharp that newcomers sneeze. Overhead, a tangle of electric wires sags between the balconies, where women hang out washing and pigeons settle on the railings.

Bargaining here is less a transaction than a performance. A buyer feigns astonishment at the price; the seller protests that he is practically giving the goods away; both enjoy the exchange, and the final figure is often settled with a smile and a cup of tea. To hurry would be to miss the point.

As the day grows hot, the crowd thickens and the noise rises to a steady roar of voices, horns and bells. Yet for all its apparent disorder, the bazaar has its own quiet logic. Every trade keeps to its lane, every vendor knows his neighbour, and beneath the din runs an ancient rhythm of buying, selling and conversation that has outlasted the centuries.

title: The Night Train
text:
The night train left the city a little after dusk, pulling slowly past the lit windows of apartment blocks and the glow of roadside tea stalls before the lights thinned and darkness took over. In my compartment, four strangers arranged their bags, exchanged cautious greetings and settled into the quiet courtesy of people who know they will spend many hours together.

Conversation began, as it often does on long journeys, with food. An elderly woman unwrapped a parcel of parathas and insisted that everyone take one; a young engineer produced a flask of tea; I offered a packet of biscuits that seemed a poor contribution beside such generosity. Within an hour, we knew one another’s destinations and occupations and the names of several grandchildren. There is a particular freedom in talking to people one will probably never meet again.

Later, when the others slept, I stood by the open door at the end of the carriage. The train was crossing a plain so flat and empty that the horizon seemed only a few steps away. The moon had risen, turning the fields to silver, and here and there the single lamp of a farmhouse burned like a solitary star that had fallen to earth. The rhythm of the wheels was steady, almost hypnotic.

By dawn, the landscape had changed entirely. Brown hills rose on either side, and at a small station a vendor passed hot tea through the window. My companions gathered their belongings, pressed on me addresses that I would never use, and stepped out into the morning. I have forgotten much of that journey, but not the sense that, for one night, a railway carriage had held a small and temporary community.

title: Address to a Graduating Class
text:
Graduates, today you leave this university with degrees that open doors. Many of you will be tempted, quite naturally, to judge your future success by the size of your salary or the height of your office. I do not ask you to ignore such ambitions. I ask only that you set beside them another question: whom will your work serve?

Some of you will enter the public service. You will find that it rarely offers applause. A clerk who processes a pension without delay, an engineer who insists that a bridge be built to the proper standard, a magistrate who hears the poorest petitioner with the same attention as the richest: none of them will appear in the newspapers. Yet it is through countless acts of this kind that citizens decide whether their state deserves their trust.

Others will work in business, medicine, teaching or law. The same principle applies. Every profession gives its members power over people who depend on their honesty and skill. A doctor’s patient, a teacher’s pupil and a lawyer’s client are rarely in a position to check what is done on their behalf. Integrity is tested precisely in such moments, when no one is watching and a shortcut would go unnoticed.

You will make mistakes; everyone does. What matters is whether you admit them and learn, or conceal them and repeat them. Remember that the knowledge you carry from this place was paid for not only by your families but by a society that hopes for something in return. Repay that hope, and whatever titles you gather along the way, you will have lived a life of real consequence. Congratulations, and go well.

subject: English
q: The passage mainly shows how Bilal:
o: became wealthy by repairing expensive clocks
learned patience and careful observation from his master
rebelled against his uncle’s wishes
invented a new kind of pocket watch
explanation: The story traces how Yusuf’s test taught the impatient Bilal to look before acting, a calm he kept throughout his own career.

subject: English
q: What was Bilal asked to do during his first month in the workshop?
o: Clean parts, sort screws and sweep the floor
Repair customers’ broken clocks
Sell watches in the lane outside
Keep the shop’s accounts
explanation: The second paragraph says he was told to clean parts, sort screws by size and sweep the floor.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, why had Bilal’s uncle sent him to Yusuf?
o: He wanted Bilal to inherit the workshop
Bilal had shown a gift for mechanics
He hoped a trade would steady the restless boy
Yusuf had asked for an assistant
explanation: Bilal was sent by an uncle who hoped a trade would steady him, since he was restless and impatient.

subject: English
q: Yusuf’s instruction ‘Do not touch it until you know’ was intended mainly to teach Bilal to:
o: avoid damaging expensive watches
work faster than other apprentices
understand a problem fully before acting on it
rely on his master for every answer
explanation: While studying the watch Bilal learned to look before acting, and later he would examine a clock before picking up his tools.

subject: English
q: The word ‘coaxing’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: roughly forcing
cheaply selling
exactly copying
gently and patiently persuading
explanation: Yusuf coaxes life back into old mechanisms, that is, restores them through gentle, patient effort.

subject: English
q: The pocket watch on the shelf in Bilal’s shop is most probably:
o: a gift from a grateful customer
the first watch he ever bought
a watch he was never able to repair
the watch he repaired as Yusuf’s apprentice
explanation: Asked where he learned patience, Bilal points to a small, battered pocket watch that keeps perfect time, recalling the stopped watch he fixed for Yusuf.

subject: English
q: The chief purpose of the passage is to:
o: argue that bazaars should be replaced by modern shops
portray the sights, sounds and customs of a traditional bazaar
explain how prices are set in international trade
record the history of a particular city
explanation: The passage describes the bazaar from dawn to midday, dwelling on its colours, smells, sounds and the custom of bargaining.

subject: English
q: Why do the shopkeepers sprinkle water in front of their stalls?
o: To cool their goods in the heat
To wash away the night’s rubbish
To settle the dust for the day
To welcome their first customers
explanation: The first paragraph says they sprinkle water on the dusty ground to settle it for the day.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, what makes newcomers sneeze?
o: The dust raised by passing handcarts
The sharp scent from the spice merchants’ sacks
The smoke from the coppersmith’s workshop
The steam rising from glasses of tea
explanation: The open sacks of turmeric, chilli and cumin fill the air with a scent so sharp that newcomers sneeze.

subject: English
q: The word ‘feigns’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: genuinely feels
pretends to show
loudly rejects
quietly hides
explanation: Bargaining is called a performance, so the buyer’s astonishment at the price is put on for effect, not real.

subject: English
q: The statement that bargaining is ‘less a transaction than a performance’ suggests that:
o: buyers and sellers dislike one another
prices in the bazaar are fixed in advance
the social enjoyment of the exchange matters as much as the price
the sellers are trained actors
explanation: Both sides enjoy the exchange and settle with a smile and tea; the writer adds that hurrying would miss the point.

subject: English
q: In the last paragraph, the writer suggests that the bazaar’s disorder is:
o: dangerous and in need of control
a recent result of overcrowding
the reason its trade has declined
only apparent, since it follows an established order
explanation: The writer says that for all its apparent disorder the bazaar has its own quiet logic: every trade keeps to its lane and every vendor knows his neighbour.

subject: English
q: What does the writer chiefly remember about the journey?
o: The discomfort of travelling through the night
A long delay at a small station
The brief sense of community among fellow passengers
The difficulty of finding food on the train
explanation: The writer says much of the journey is forgotten, but not the sense that the carriage had held a small and temporary community.

subject: English
q: According to the passage, how did conversation among the passengers begin?
o: With a discussion of the scenery
With complaints about the train
With the sharing of food
With an exchange of addresses
explanation: The second paragraph says conversation began, as it often does on long journeys, with food.

subject: English
q: To what does the writer compare the lamps of the farmhouses?
o: The lit windows of city apartments
The glow of roadside tea stalls
The silver light of the moon
Solitary stars fallen to earth
explanation: The third paragraph says the single lamp of a farmhouse burned like a solitary star that had fallen to earth.

subject: English
q: The word ‘hypnotic’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: lulling, as if inducing a trance
irregular and jarring
loud and alarming
fast and exciting
explanation: The steady rhythm of the wheels at night, while the others slept, had a soothing, trance-like effect.

subject: English
q: The phrase ‘addresses that I would never use’ implies that:
o: the passengers had given false addresses
the writer disliked the other passengers
the addresses were in a script the writer could not read
the friendships of the journey were not expected to continue
explanation: Earlier the writer notes the freedom of talking to people one will never meet again; the community of the carriage was “temporary”.

subject: English
q: The tone of the passage is best described as:
o: anxious and hurried
reflective and warm
bitter and critical
formal and technical
explanation: The writer looks back fondly on the generosity of strangers and the quiet beauty of the night journey.

subject: English
q: The central message of the speech is that graduates should:
o: reject all ambitions for salary and position
enter the public service rather than business
measure success partly by the service their work gives to others
avoid professions that give power over others
explanation: The speaker does not dismiss ambition but asks graduates to set beside it the question of whom their work will serve.

subject: English
q: According to the speaker, public servants who do their work well:
o: are frequently praised in the newspapers
rarely receive public recognition
are paid more than other professionals
seldom face difficult decisions
explanation: The speaker says public service rarely offers applause and that such officials will not appear in the newspapers.

subject: English
q: Why, according to the speaker, is integrity tested in the professions?
o: Professionals are closely watched by their clients
Every profession is strictly regulated by the state
Shortcuts are always discovered in the end
Those who depend on professionals are rarely able to check their work
explanation: Patients, pupils and clients are rarely in a position to check what is done for them, so integrity is tested when no one is watching.

subject: English
q: The word ‘conceal’, as used in the passage, most nearly means:
o: hide
admit
correct
forget
explanation: The speaker contrasts admitting mistakes with concealing them, so conceal means to hide.

subject: English
q: By saying that graduates’ knowledge was paid for ‘by a society that hopes for something in return’, the speaker suggests that they:
o: must repay their tuition fees to the state
were educated entirely at public expense
owe a debt of service to the wider community
should work abroad to earn higher salaries
explanation: The speaker urges graduates to “repay that hope” through their work, implying an obligation of service rather than a financial debt.

subject: English
q: The tone of the speech is best described as:
o: sarcastic and dismissive
anxious and fearful
earnest and inspiring
boastful and self-congratulatory
explanation: The speaker sincerely encourages graduates towards service and integrity and closes with warm congratulations.
